html:
1Core Concepts and Definitions

Purpose of the domain: plan for and use the available resources effectively and efficiently, so the right resources are in the right place at the right time and amount. It covers people and physical or virtual resources, and their availability, utilization and maintenance.

Term Meaning
Project manager Leads the team: forms it, makes it work as a group, develops skills and motivation, acts ethically; aware of environment, locations, politics, culture and organizational change
Resource manager A person with management authority over one or more resources (for example a functional manager). The project team may not control selection (collective agreements, subcontractors, matrix environments)
Human resources (team members) Individuals with assigned roles and responsibilities working to a shared goal; usually top-down (centralized) leadership, but teams may self-organize (distributed leadership)
Physical, material or virtual resources Anything that is not a person: equipment, materials, supplies, facilities, infrastructure, software, testing environments, licenses, services, information or documents
Internal vs external resources Internal: assigned by functional or resource managers. External: obtained through partnerships, joint ventures or procurement (Topic 22)
Role / responsibility / authority / competence Role: the function assigned. Responsibility: the work expected. Authority: the right to apply resources, decide, sign approvals and accept deliverables (should match responsibility). Competence: skill and capacity to do the work
Resource requirements Types and quantities of resources for each work package or activity; aggregated for each WBS branch and the project; include assumptions on availability
Resource breakdown structure (RBS) Hierarchy of resources by category (labor, materials, equipment, supplies) and type (skill level, grade, certification)
Resource calendar The working days, shifts, holidays and periods when each specific resource is available
Team charter The team's values, agreements and operating guidelines
Skill matrix Maps skills required against skills available to expose gaps
Preassignment Resources determined in advance (named in a proposal, or needed for specific expertise, or assigned in Initiating)
Virtual team / colocation Virtual: a team with little or no face-to-face time. Colocation: members physically close to improve communication and productivity
Centralized vs distributed management and leadership Centralized: decisions and authority held by a few senior leaders, accountability usually with one individual (the PM). Distributed: decision-making and authority spread among individuals and teams; project management work may be shared or the team may self-organize

2The Five Resource Processes

Process Focus area Purpose Key outputs Decision tools
Plan Resource Management Planning (once or at defined points) Define the approach and level of management effort for estimating, acquiring, leading and using resources, based on type and complexity; consider scarce or competed-for resources Resource management plan, team charter Responsibility assignment matrix, hierarchical charts, text-oriented formats, organizational theory, green HRM, resource-based view, SWOT, interviews
Estimate Resources Planning (once or at defined points) Identify the type, quantity and characteristics of team and physical or virtual resources for the work; anticipate shortages or surpluses Resource requirements, basis of estimates, resource breakdown structure Expert judgment, bottom-up, analogous, parametric, alternative analysis, PMIS; also AI, predictive analytics, branch and bound, genetic algorithms, COCOMO
Acquire Resources Executing (periodic) Obtain and assign the team and physical or virtual resources Resource and team assignments, updated resource calendars, change requests Multicriteria decision analysis, negotiation, problem-solving, preassignment, virtual teams
Lead the Team Executing Guide, develop and manage the team through feedback, collaboration, conflict resolution and escalation (Topic 25) Team performance assessments, change requests Colocation, virtual teams, conflict management, influencing, motivation, team building, coaching, recognition, retrospectives
Monitor and Control Resourcing Monitoring & Controlling (continuous) Ensure assigned physical or virtual resources are available as planned, compare planned with actual use, correct as needed, release when done Work performance information, change requests Alternative analysis, cost-benefit analysis, performance reviews, trend analysis, negotiation, influencing, value stream mapping, theory of constraints, control charts

3Plan Resource Management (ECO: define and plan resources based on requirements)

3.1 The resource management plan

Describes how resources are acquired, allocated, monitored and controlled; it may split into a team management plan and a physical resource management plan.

Element What it defines
Identification of resources How team and physical resources are identified and quantified
Acquiring resources How to obtain team and physical resources (including the sourcing route, for example a PMO pool)
Roles and responsibilities Role, authority, responsibility, competence (what skills, and what to do about gaps: training, hiring, schedule or scope changes)
Project organization charts Graphic of members and reporting relationships (formal or informal, detailed to fit the size)
Project team resource management How team resources are defined, staffed, managed and finally released
Training Training strategies
Team development Methods for developing the team
Resource control Managing inventory, equipment and supplies; optimizing acquisition of physical resources
Recognition plan Which recognitions and rewards, and when

3.2 Tools

Tool Use
Responsibility assignment matrix (RAM) Grid linking work packages or activities to resources; shows all work of one person and all people on one activity; only one person accountable per task. RACI (responsible, accountable, consulted, informed) is a common form and helps when internal and external resources mix
Hierarchical charts OBS (organizational units that perform the work), WBS (deliverables), RBS (resources by category and type), VBS (WBS with value estimates)
Text-oriented formats Position descriptions and role-responsibility-authority forms: responsibilities, authority, competencies, qualifications; reusable templates
Organizational theory How people, teams and units behave; supports a flexible leadership style that adapts to team maturity; structure and culture shape the project structure
Green human resource management People practices that favor sustainable use of resources and environmental performance (recruitment, training, performance management, rewards)
Resource-based view Identify strategic resources that give competitive advantage; evaluate with VRIO (value, rarity, imitability, organization)
SWOT, interviews Assess strengths and weaknesses of resources and gather needs
Skill matrix Compare required and available skills; keep it current

3.3 The team charter

A document of the team's values, communication guidelines, decision-making criteria and processes, conflict resolution processes, meeting guidelines and team agreements.

  • Works best when the team creates it (or at least contributes); all members share responsibility for following it.
  • Review and update it periodically and when new members join, so they help shape the ground rules.
  • Early agreement on conduct, communication and decision-making reduces misunderstandings and raises productivity.

4Estimate Resources

  • Estimate for each work package or activity the type, quantity and characteristics (skills, grade, certification) of people and physical or virtual resources. Equipment, materials, test environments and licenses must be estimated with the labor, not as an afterthought (and with lead times).
  • Inputs include the resource management plan, schedule, scope baseline, activity attributes, cost estimates and resource calendars. The process is closely tied to Estimate Costs and the schedule: align resource, cost and duration estimates (Topics 16 and 17).
  • Techniques: expert judgment, bottom-up, analogous, parametric (Topic 14), alternative analysis (options such as make or buy, different resource mixes), PMIS; PMBOK 8 also lists AI, predictive analytics, branch and bound and genetic algorithms for optimization, and COCOMO for software.
  • Outputs: resource requirements (with assumptions on availability and quantity), basis of estimates, RBS.
  • Benefit: anticipate shortages and surpluses and manage allocation and utilization risk.

5Acquire Resources (ECO: manage and optimize resource needs and availability)

  • Collaborate, negotiate and influence the people who can provide resources (functional or resource managers, suppliers, partners).
  • Follow the sourcing route in the resource management plan (for example, specialized roles come through the PMO pool) rather than bypassing it.
  • Preassigned resources come with their own availability; plan with the actual availability shown in resource calendars.
  • Virtual teams widen the pool (distributed locations, shifts, home offices, people with mobility limitations, avoiding travel cost), but need more planning of communication, clear expectations, conflict protocols, cultural understanding and shared credit.
  • Colocation (temporary or full) improves communication; use a team room and visible schedules.
  • Multicriteria decision analysis helps choose among candidates or sources.
  • If a resource is not available (economic factors, assignment to other projects): assign an alternative with different competencies, features or cost only if risks are acknowledged and legal, regulatory or mandatory criteria are not violated; document the effect on schedule, budget, risks, quality and training plans.
  • Failing to acquire resources raises risk and can hurt schedule, budget, quality and satisfaction, and in the worst case cancel the project.
  • Agile: teams work best with dedicated, cross-functional members; part-time or shared members cause context switching and waiting.

6Optimize Resource Needs and Availability

Situation Response
Over-allocation on non-critical work Resource smoothing within float (end date unchanged); then leveling if needed (Topic 16)
Over-allocation on the critical path Leveling may delay the finish; evaluate adding capacity, reassigning, resequencing or reducing scope, with cost and risk analysis and change control
Skill gap Use the skill matrix: training, coaching, mentoring, hiring, contracting, schedule or scope changes, chosen by time, cost and risk
Competing demand from other projects or operations Negotiate with the resource owner and other project managers; escalate through governance (Topic 12); show shared resources in the schedule
Resource idle or no longer needed Release it on time (reassign or end the agreement) to avoid cost
Capacity changes (agile) Plan iterations on actual available capacity, not on the original assumption; do not squeeze the team to keep the scope
Well-being and engagement Watch workload and signs such as burnout or "quiet quitting" (minimum effort, silence in meetings, absenteeism); adjust the plan and support well-being (flexible schedules, stress management, time off)
Sustainability Consider environmental and social impact across the value chain (hiring, materials sourcing, transport, disposal); green HRM

Utilization indicators (PMBOK 8 Table 2-10): actual versus planned resource use, total downtime versus planned resource time, units produced versus hours worked (or cost of work performed versus scheduled time), and materials used, scrap and rework as signs of efficient use.

7Monitor and Control Resourcing

Concerned with physical and virtual resources (team members are handled in Lead the Team). It runs continuously.

  • Monitor resource expenditures and planned versus actual use.
  • Identify and deal with shortages and surpluses in good time.
  • Ensure resources are used and released per plan and project need.
  • Inform stakeholders of resource issues; influence the factors that change utilization; manage changes as they occur.
  • Risks of poor control: missing critical equipment delays production; low-quality materials cause rework and recalls; too much inventory raises cost, too little blocks delivery.
  • Tools: alternative analysis, cost-benefit analysis, performance reviews, trend analysis, problem-solving, negotiation, influencing, PMIS, value stream mapping, theory of constraints, continuous improvement, control charts.
  • Outputs: work performance information, change requests, updates to the resource plan, baselines, assignments, risk register and lessons learned.

8Leading the Team (summary; detail in Topic 25)

  • Lead the Team applies management (processes, planning, coordination, measuring) and leadership (influencing, motivating, listening, enabling) to improve competencies, interactions and the team environment; adjust style to team willingness and ability.
  • Common aspects of team development: vision and objectives, roles and responsibilities, team operations (charter, norms), guidance, growth.
  • High-performing teams show open communication, shared understanding, shared ownership, trust, collaboration, adaptability, resilience, empowerment and autonomy, and recognition.
  • Project manager role-modeling (PMBOK 8): transparency (including about bias), integrity, respect, positive discourse (dialogue rather than debate), support, courage, and celebrating success.
  • Outputs include team performance assessments: improvements in skills and competencies, lower turnover, higher cohesion.

9Predictive vs Agile vs Hybrid

Predictive Agile / adaptive Hybrid
Planning Requirements and allocation defined early from the schedule; detailed resource management plan; availability secured throughout Self-organizing, collaborative teams of generalizing specialists; plans less predictable; flexible agreements Predictive for fixed or specialist resources; adaptive teams for variable work
Team structure Functional or matrix; roles formalized; RAM Stable, dedicated, cross-functional teams, often about 3 to 9 members; product owner and facilitator roles Mix
Leadership Centralized; more direction when new to the work Distributed or servant leadership; team decides how to do the work Mix
Capacity Schedule-driven allocation, leveling and smoothing Capacity-based iteration planning; fixed team, flexed scope Both
Control Planned vs actual use; histograms; utilization Team velocity and capacity; impediment removal Both
Beyond PMBOK 8 T-shaped skills and swarming

10Tailoring, Interactions and Checking Results

Tailoring considerations (PMBOK 8 §2.6.3): development approach; maturity of team culture (cross-organization teams need more up-front work to build a "one team" mindset); team culture, bias and the project manager's role-modeling; industry context (lean, just-in-time, Kaizen, total productive maintenance, theory of constraints; use the organization's methods); governance structures (centralized or distributed authority); sustainability; maturity of team members (less oversight for mature teams); virtual teams; employee well-being.

PMBOK 8 examples: (1) a large high-variability adaptive project has less predictable resource planning and needs flexible agreements and lean methods; (2) a new virtual team has collaboration problems, so provide collaboration sites and a team site, use audio and video, keep ongoing contact by messaging, schedule time to get to know remote members, hold at least one face-to-face meeting, and create a team charter with ways of working.

Interactions: the domain touches all others. Other projects may compete for the same resources at the same time and place. Resource estimates align with cost estimates; resource availability shapes the schedule; the risk and stakeholder domains also influence outcomes.

Check results (Table 2-10):

Outcome Check
Shared ownership; high-performing team Members know the vision; own deliverables; trust, collaborate, adapt, feel empowered and recognized
Effective resource utilization Actual vs planned use managed
Acceptable downtime Total downtime vs planned resource time
Productive team Units produced vs hours worked; KPIs reviewed
Efficient physical or virtual resource management Materials used, scrap and rework
Resource procurement managed Efficiency checks, order, manufacture and delivery tracking

11Exam Traps and What PMI Expects

  1. Resources are people and things. Estimate equipment, materials, test environments and licenses with the labor.
  2. One accountable person per activity in the RAM or RACI.
  3. Follow the resource management plan's sourcing route (for example the PMO pool) instead of bypassing it.
  4. Alternatives are allowed only within legal and regulatory limits and with documented impacts; never skip a mandatory qualification to save time.
  5. Authority must match responsibility. Where authority is missing (functional or weak matrix), negotiate and align the managers; escalate if they cannot agree.
  6. Preassigned resources: use their real availability in estimates and schedule.
  7. Smooth within float first; leveling may move the end date; critical-path over-allocation needs analysis and change control.
  8. Plan agile iterations on actual capacity. Do not hold the scope and ask the team to work harder.
  9. Dedicated, cross-functional agile team members beat part-time shared ones.
  10. Skill gaps: use the skill matrix and choose training, coaching, hiring or contracting by time, cost and risk; update the plan.
  11. The team charter is co-created and revisited when members join; do not hand a new member a rulebook privately.
  12. Release resources when no longer needed and track planned vs actual use; idle resources are cost.
  13. Watch well-being: signs of burnout need a plan and scope or capacity change, not more overtime incentives.
  14. Virtual teams need deliberate setup: team charter, collaboration tools, relationship-building time and a face-to-face meeting where possible.
  15. Shared resources across projects need coordination, not unilateral booking.
  16. Compare planned and actual usage and fix shortages or surpluses early; inventory too high or too low both cost value.

12Exam Q&A

12.1 Scenario questions (choose the best answer)

S1The skill matrix shows that no one on the agile team can perform security testing, which is due to start in eight weeks. What should the project manager do?

  • ARemove security testing from the scope to protect the schedule
  • BWait until the testing is due and then look for an available specialist
  • CCompare training, hiring and contracting on time, cost and risk, then update the plan
  • DAssign the security testing to the most experienced developer and hope for the best
Show the answer

Answer: C. A skill matrix exposes gaps, and the response (training, coaching, hiring, contracting, or schedule and scope changes) is chosen by time, cost and risk and then reflected in the plan. Assigning an unqualified person, dropping the test or waiting leaves the gap unmanaged.

S2The certified welder assigned to a pressure-vessel job is unavailable, and an uncertified colleague could start immediately. What should the project manager do?

  • AObtain a qualified alternative, because a mandatory certification cannot be skipped
  • BDelay the job for as long as it takes for the original welder to return
  • CAssign the colleague and have a certified welder sign off the finished work
  • DAssign the colleague now and arrange his certification during the job
Show the answer

Answer: A. An alternative resource may be used only if risks are acknowledged and no legal, regulatory or mandatory criteria are violated, so a required certification cannot be waived to save time. Signing off later, certifying during the job or waiting indefinitely either breaches the requirement or ignores workable options.

S3The proposal named a specific architect as a preassigned resource, but his calendar shows he is only 50% available for the next three months. How should the project manager plan?

  • AReplace him immediately with an architect who is available full time
  • BUse his actual availability in the estimates and schedule, and address the gap
  • CKeep the plan unchanged and compress the schedule to compensate later
  • DPlan with full availability as promised in the proposal and expect him to adjust
Show the answer

Answer: B. Preassigned resources come with their own availability, and plans use the actual availability shown in the resource calendars. Planning on the promised full time, replacing a named person without analysis or compressing later builds the gap into the plan.

S4The responsibility assignment matrix shows one team member as responsible for 28 activities in the same two-week window. What does this show, and what should the project manager do?

  • AA sign of a strong performer who should keep the work as assigned
  • BA formatting problem to correct by merging the activities into one row
  • CAn accountability conflict resolved by naming a second accountable person
  • DAn overload to rebalance by reassigning work or adjusting the schedule
Show the answer

Answer: D. A RAM shows all the work assigned to one person, so a pile-up reveals overload that is rebalanced through reassignment, leveling or schedule changes. Accepting it, merging rows or adding accountable owners does not fix the capacity problem.

S5Members of a scrum team are doing the minimum, staying silent in retrospectives and starting to miss days, and the sponsor suggests overtime bonuses. What should the project manager do?

  • AOffer the bonuses so that the team works additional hours to recover
  • BReplace the quietest members with new people to bring in fresh energy
  • CAdd a weekly reporting meeting in which each member's hours are monitored
  • DAssess workload and well-being with the team, and adjust capacity or scope
Show the answer

Answer: D. Minimum effort, silence and absenteeism are signs of burnout or disengagement, which need a plan that adjusts workload and supports well-being, not more overtime incentives. Bonuses, replacing members or closer monitoring add pressure instead of addressing the cause.

S6Two test engineers have been idle for three weeks while a delayed deliverable is awaited by the hybrid program, yet they remain assigned to the project. What should the project manager do?

  • AReassign or release them for now and plan their return when needed
  • BAsk them to document expected test results before the deliverable exists
  • CKeep them on the project in case the deliverable arrives earlier than expected
  • DMove them to another project without agreement from its manager
Show the answer

Answer: A. Idle resources are cost, so they are released or reassigned and brought back when needed, with planned against actual use tracked. Keeping them idle, moving them without agreement or inventing work is wasteful or unauthorized.

S7A warehouse holds nine months of materials ordered early for the project, tying up cash and storage space. What should the project manager do?

  • AKeep the stock, since too much inventory is always safer than too little
  • BReturn all the materials and re-order them each week as the work needs them
  • CLeave the stock until closure and write off any unused remainder then
  • DCompare planned and actual usage, adjust the orders and release the surplus
Show the answer

Answer: D. Monitoring resources means comparing planned with actual use, and both too much and too little inventory cost value, so the project manager adjusts orders and releases the surplus. Keeping everything, returning everything or waiting until closure ignores the signals.

S8The project manager needs to organize labor, equipment and materials by category and by type, such as skill level or certification, to estimate and track them. Which chart fits?

  • AA RACI matrix of responsible, accountable, consulted and informed roles
  • BA resource breakdown structure of categories and types
  • CAn organizational breakdown structure of the units performing the work
  • DA work breakdown structure of deliverables and work packages
Show the answer

Answer: B. The resource breakdown structure organizes resources by category and type. The organizational breakdown structure maps the units doing the work, the WBS maps deliverables and the RACI matrix assigns roles to activities.

S9Testing is a bottleneck because only two members can test, while several developers wait for feedback. Which team design approach would help most?

  • AHire two specialist testers and keep every other role in the team unchanged
  • BAsk the developers to work on other projects until the testing capacity improves
  • CBroaden skills so developers can also test and the team can swarm on bottlenecks
  • DMove the testing to the end of the project so that developers stop waiting
Show the answer

Answer: C. Agile teams favor generalizing specialists, with T-shaped skills and swarming, so the team can flex around a bottleneck. Adding single-skill specialists, lending developers elsewhere or postponing testing keeps the dependency or delays feedback.

S10Three contractors could supply a needed specialist, differing in cost, experience and availability, and stakeholders disagree on which to pick. Which technique gives a defendable choice?

  • AMulticriteria decision analysis with agreed criteria and weights
  • BChoosing the cheapest contractor, since cost is the easiest criterion to measure
  • CA majority vote among the stakeholders without any defined criteria
  • DAsking the sponsor to pick a contractor without stating the reasons
Show the answer

Answer: A. Multicriteria decision analysis scores each option against agreed, weighted criteria, giving a transparent and defendable choice. A vote without criteria, the cheapest price alone or an unexplained pick lacks that basis.

12.2 Recall Q&As

R1Name the five Resources processes.

Show the answer

Plan Resource Management, Estimate Resources, Acquire Resources, Lead the Team, Monitor and Control Resourcing.

R2What kinds of resources does the domain cover?

Show the answer

People (team members) and physical or virtual resources: equipment, materials, supplies, facilities, infrastructure, software, test environments, licenses, services, information or documents.

R3What does the resource management plan contain?

Show the answer

Identification and acquisition of resources, roles and responsibilities (including authority and competence), organization charts, team resource management, training, team development, resource control and a recognition plan.

R4What does a team charter include?

Show the answer

Team values, communication guidelines, decision-making criteria and processes, conflict resolution processes, meeting guidelines and team agreements.

R5What is a RACI matrix and what is its key rule?

Show the answer

A responsibility assignment matrix coding each activity's people as responsible, accountable, consulted or informed; only one accountable person per activity.

R6OBS versus WBS versus RBS?

Show the answer

OBS arranges work by organizational unit; WBS breaks down deliverables; RBS lists resources by category and type.

R7What are resource requirements, the resource calendar and the RBS?

Show the answer

Requirements: types and quantities needed per work package; calendar: when each resource is available; RBS: hierarchy of resources by category and type.

R8What are preassignment, virtual teams and colocation?

Show the answer

Preassignment: resources fixed in advance; virtual teams: groups working with little face-to-face contact; colocation: members physically close together.

R9What if a needed resource is unavailable?

Show the answer

Assign an alternative (possibly different competence or cost) only if risks are acknowledged and legal or regulatory criteria are met; document the effect on schedule, budget, risks, quality and training.

R10Resource leveling versus smoothing?

Show the answer

Leveling adjusts dates to fit supply and may change the critical path and end date; smoothing uses float only and leaves both unchanged.

R11Resource manager versus project manager?

Show the answer

The resource manager has management authority over resources; the project manager leads the project team and negotiates for resources.

R12What is a skill matrix for?

Show the answer

Comparing required with available skills to find gaps to address through training, coaching, hiring or contracting.

R13What does Monitor and Control Resourcing watch?

Show the answer

Availability and planned versus actual use of physical and virtual resources, shortages and surpluses, timely release, and the cost effects of inventory and supply problems.

R14Centralized versus distributed management and leadership?

Show the answer

Centralized: authority with a few senior leaders and accountability with one individual; distributed: decisions and authority spread among individuals and teams, possibly self-organizing.

13Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Processes Plan Resource Mgmt → Estimate Resources → Acquire Resources → Lead the Team → Monitor and Control Resourcing
Resource types People and physical or virtual resources (equipment, materials, licenses, test environments, services, information)
Resource management plan Identification, acquisition, roles (authority, responsibility, competence), org charts, release, training, development, control, recognition
Team charter Values, communication, decisions, conflict, meetings, agreements; co-created; update when members join

Hierarchical charts OBS, WBS, RBS, VBS

Acquire Negotiate and influence; follow the sourcing route; preassignment; virtual teams; alternatives only within legal limits
Optimize Smooth within float, then level; address skill gaps; plan agile iterations on actual capacity; release idle resources
Skill gaps Skill matrix → training, coaching, hiring, contracting, schedule or scope change
Monitor and control Planned vs actual use, shortages, surplus, release, inventory
Authority Matches responsibility; weak or functional structures: negotiate with functional managers
Agile teams Dedicated, cross-functional, about 3 to 9, capacity-based planning, distributed leadership

Well-being Burnout and quiet quitting are signals; adjust the plan and support the team
